In one of the most tense and consequential encounters in Oval Office history, President Trump and Vice President JD Vance in February 2025 teamed up on Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky.

   It was taught and riveting, like watching an extended, grueling tennis volley (although the stakes were much, much greater).

   “This is going to be great television,” Trump said at the time, as cameras broadcast the encounter around the world.

   On Monday, the television rotation that brought the exchange to life effectively went dark. Trump blocked CNN from the pool of reporters that travels with the president. There are four other networks in the TV pool with CNN, and they said Monday they would no longer participate. And just like that, the cameras disappeared.

   Pool cameras have captured history for decades (President Bush and White House chief of staff Andy Card at a school on Sept. 11, 2001, to cite one memorable moment).

   In an example of how confusing this all will be, Trump had a ribbon-cutting Monday for a new White House helipad. Video of the event streamed on the White House website showed him speaking to supporters, but there weren’t any microphones to pick up his remarks. But Monday afternoon, a press conference with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was carried live on CNN. Mamdani said he told the president that all media would be allowed to cover the press conference.

   “They said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me,” Trump said, waving his arm toward the cameras.

   After it was announced that Trump would be leaving the press conference, he stayed and kept answering questions.

   The president is scheduled Tuesday to give an address at the United Nations in New York, which will likely be very newsworthy. Will the only cameras there be those run by the U.N. and governments?

   In an irony that could only happen during Trump’s second term, one of the first meetings these cameras (and therefore, the country) will miss is one scheduled between Trump and Zelensky. And there are many more meetings this week at the U.N. General Assembly that Trump is scheduled to have, not to mention his coming summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

   Six weeks before the midterm elections—with high gas prices, uncertainty in the Middle East and the Ukraine war—all eyes were on Trump’s every move. He has lost one of his primary windows to voters, business leaders and his foreign counterparts.

Trump’s Second Term Is Made-for-TV, but the Cameras Have Clicked Off
 
Plus, Bill Pulte checked on Todd Blanche’s mortgages, and vulnerable Republican candidates call for export ban on diesel
 
 
FINN GOMEZ/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. In one of the most tense and consequential encounters in Oval Office history, President Trump and Vice President JD Vance in February 2025 teamed up on Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky.

 

It was taught and riveting, like watching an extended, grueling tennis volley (although the stakes were much, much greater).

 

“This is going to be great television,” Trump said at the time, as cameras broadcast the encounter around the world.

 

On Monday, the television rotation that brought the exchange to life effectively went dark. Trump blocked CNN from the pool of reporters that travels with the president. There are four other networks in the TV pool with CNN, and they said Monday they would no longer participate. And just like that, the cameras disappeared.

 

Pool cameras have captured history for decades (President Bush and White House chief of staff Andy Card at a school on Sept. 11, 2001, to cite one memorable moment).

 

In an example of how confusing this all will be, Trump had a ribbon-cutting Monday for a new White House helipad. Video of the event streamed on the White House website showed him speaking to supporters, but there weren’t any microphones to pick up his remarks. But Monday afternoon, a press conference with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was carried live on CNN. Mamdani said he told the president that all media would be allowed to cover the press conference.

 

“They said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me,” Trump said, waving his arm toward the cameras.

 

After it was announced that Trump would be leaving the press conference, he stayed and kept answering questions.

 

The president is scheduled Tuesday to give an address at the United Nations in New York, which will likely be very newsworthy. Will the only cameras there be those run by the U.N. and governments?

 

In an irony that could only happen during Trump’s second term, one of the first meetings these cameras (and therefore, the country) will miss is one scheduled between Trump and Zelensky. And there are many more meetings this week at the U.N. General Assembly that Trump is scheduled to have, not to mention his coming summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

 

Six weeks before the midterm elections—with high gas prices, uncertainty in the Middle East and the Ukraine war—all eyes were on Trump’s every move. He has lost one of his primary windows to voters, business leaders and his foreign counterparts.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

United Nations General Assembly: World leaders and thousands of foreign officials will meet in New York City as the general debate opens at the annual gathering.

 

Trump’s Tuesday: The president is set to address the assembly this morning. Then throughout the day he will meet with the following leaders: U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Prime Minister of Japan Sanae Takaichi, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Acting President of Venezuela Delcy Rodríguez.

What I’m Following

 
 
BONNIE CASH/PRESS POOL
 

Housing chief Bill Pulte looked at Attorney General Todd Blanche’s mortgages. The check came as Pulte was examining the mortgages of Trump’s adversaries. Some officials thought Pulte had been trying to collect information on Blanche, then No. 2 at the DOJ, and others to pressure them to more quickly pursue investigations, according to people familiar with the matter.

 

Trump has repeatedly discussed kicking the entire press corps out of the White House. He raised the matter as recently as last month, as his frustrations grew with media coverage, according to current and former administration officials. Some of his advisers have cautioned against the move, and a senior administration official said the president had no plans to banish the press from the White House.

 

Republican candidates in tight races are calling for an export ban on diesel. They are running out of time to calm voters angry about rising fuel costs, setting off a scramble on an issue many see as the GOP’s biggest political liability in the midterms. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R., Iowa), who is locked in a close race with Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for an open Senate seat in Iowa, argued that Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.”

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• OpenAI asked Washington to lead an effort with other countries to develop global safety and security standards for building cutting-edge AI.

 

• The Trump administration has proposed investing $5 billion in a new fund that would help Middle East countries rebuild war-battered energy infrastructure and trim their reliance on the Strait of Hormuz to transport oil and gas.

 

• There were more good vibes for ideological foes Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who had another friendly meeting on Monday.
